name: Tree benefits
seoTitle: Tree benefits Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Tree benefits: work out period of time from number of trees and the carbon stored. A free ecology calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Tree benefits calculator number of trees and the carbon stored and it returns period of time. It suits a footprint, a resource or an environmental change you want to size up. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Tree benefits calculator work?
sections.html:
The Tree benefits calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports period of time in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the tree type and the circumference); then you type in number of trees and the carbon stored.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 8 options, such as mixed, oak and douglas fir. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 8 options, such as <7.9 in, 7.9–19.7 in and 20.1–35.4 in. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in kilograms. The unit chip switches it to any of the 29 supported units.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Tree benefits calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Period of time=2 × carbon stored ÷ (number of trees × (diameter (at breast height), tree type))
Plane distance=(100 ÷ 9) × carbon stored
Oxygen produced=(8 ÷ 3) × carbon stored
Oxygen produced=(21 ÷ 25) × people daily oxygen
Water evaporated=450 × period of time × number of trees
Time air conditioners=20 × period of time × number of trees

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in centimeters

  • Time, opening in years
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Volume, opening in liters
  • Length, opening in meters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Tree benefits calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — number of trees and the carbon stored — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Tree benefits calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns period of time, derived from number of trees and the carbon stored. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Tree benefits calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for number of trees and the carbon stored, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter custom circumference in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Custom circumference opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Custom circumference = 0 cm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Tree benefits calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
